extracted.intended_audience: administrative-law scholars, democratic theorists, and policymakers interested in the legitimacy of administrative processes
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative criteria and normative standards for how administrative processes (especially notice-and-comment rulemaking) should produce democratically legitimate outcomes, drawing on pluralist, civic-republican, deliberative, and minimalist democratic theories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fair competition among interests
rubrics_metrics.description: The competition for policy must be a 'fair fight' rather than biased by differences in the distribution of incentives to compete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pluralist critiques emphasize that differences in resources and incentives produce uneven competition; neopluralists therefore recommend adapting policymaking processes to expand opportunities to participate in government decision making (a 'polyarchy'). The criterion implies evaluating whether participatory procedures balance opportunities across interests and do not systematically advantage better-resourced actors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent informational/industry capture
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid informational capture in which regulated entities overload participatory processes with resources and expertise so that regulation is 'acquired by the industry' and 'designed and operated primarily for its benefit.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for tactics where regulated parties dominate notice-and-comment or other participatory fora through resource-intensive submissions, expert overload, or lobbying (including during centralized review like OIRA). Procedural designs should limit opportunities for such capture or otherwise counterbalance concentrated informational advantages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privileging dialectical deliberation (deliberative quality)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ideal form of participation is the dialectic process of offering reasons that are then subjected to critical engagement; this form should be privileged so a consensus about the common good can emerge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate processes by whether they foster reason-giving, critical engagement, and conditions for consensus formation (e.g., structured deliberations, deliberative polls, minipublics). Recognize that privileging deliberative engagement implies excluding or deprioritizing forms of participation that do not approximate reasoned debate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public reason constraints on acceptable reasons
rubrics_metrics.description: Deliberation about fundamental questions of government should be limited to 'public reason'—reasons that all citizens may reasonably be expected to endorse—excluding 'comprehensive doctrines' that cannot be accepted by all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether participatory and justificatory norms constrain arguments to publicly shareable reasons (Rawls/Habermas-style) and whether those constraints are justified or unduly exclusionary. Consider anti-patterns where exclusion of certain moral or religious perspectives renders deliberation unrepresentative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scalability of deliberative methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods proven at small scale (minipublics, deliberative polls) may not be easily scalable to mass participation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proposing deliberative reforms to notice-and-comment or regulatory participation, evaluate whether techniques that work in small, structured settings can be implemented at society-wide scale and what losses in deliberative quality or inclusiveness might follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost–Benefit Analysis as a republican, universalizing decision rule
rubrics_metrics.description: CBA purports to abstract regulatory analysis to synoptic rationality, yielding a decision rule to do things that increase net social benefits after considering social costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether reliance on CBA operationalizes a conception of the common good and whether executive/institutional commitments (e.g., Executive Orders 12291, 12866; OIRA review) align regulatory decisions with that decision rule. Also evaluate treatment of unquantified benefits and distributional effects—whether CBA used narrowly or adapted to consider equity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centralized review to coordinate regulatory activities (OIRA role)
rubrics_metrics.description: Central review (OIRA) can coordinate federal regulatory activity and align it with standards of the common good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether centralized review improves coordination and normative grounding of rules, but also be attentive to concerns about lobbying of the review office and elite capture of that coordination function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimal conditions for legitimate deliberation (procedural minimalism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given critiques that full deliberative ideals are unrealistic/restrictive, legitimacy may require a minimalist set of conditions that are feasible to achieve in practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate participatory processes against a defensible, minimal set of deliberative conditions (e.g., impartial facilitation, inclusion of diverse voices, opportunities for reason-giving) rather than maximal idealized lists that are unattainable in mass administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge issues unsuited to deliberation; require mutual respect and provisionality
rubrics_metrics.description: For some ethical or conscience-laden issues, deliberation cannot bridge deep value divergence; in such cases the appropriate democratic posture is mutual respect and accommodation, and decisions should be provisional and open to future challenge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When regulating on deeply contested moral matters, evaluate legitimacy in light of whether agencies treat decisions as provisional, create space for accommodation, and avoid imposing a falsely consensual rationale that masks persistent disagreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electoral accountability as a democratic baseline (minimalism/Schumpeterian test)
rubrics_metrics.description: Democracy can be defended as an institutional arrangement wherein individuals acquire power to decide by competitive struggle for votes; regular elections and majority-rule mechanisms provide core democratic legitimacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess administrative arrangements for whether they preserve pathways for electoral accountability (e.g., majoritarian control over policy direction) and whether the electoral mechanism effectively counteracts domination over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative accountability to elected officials (structural design)
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrative decisions should be subject to lines of accountability to elected officials (appointments, for-cause removal doctrines, presidential oversight) so that the unelected bureaucracy is responsive to democratic control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate institutional features—appointment power, removal rules, presidential administration practices, and doctrines that constrain agency insulation—for how well they tether administrative outputs to electorally accountable actors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial review intensity keyed to risk of domination
rubrics_metrics.description: The intensity of judicial review should be calibrated to the risk of domination posed by agency action: 'thin rationality' is appropriate most of the time, but courts should increase scrutiny when fundamental interests or risks of domination are implicated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether courts apply a sliding scale of review—using ordinary deference where stakes are low but ramping up arbitrariness review when vulnerable groups or core rights are at risk (illustrated by increased scrutiny in the DACA decision).

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional ability to identify and reflect the demos' working consensus (legitimacy metric)
rubrics_metrics.description: Democratic institutions, including the administrative state, should be judged by their capacity to identify the will of the demos and make policies that reflect a working consensus (however defined).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as a high-level evaluative yardstick: do administrative procedures (notice-and-comment, hearings, review) produce policies that citizens view as responsive and therefore legitimate? If not, theorists argue the institution fails democratically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice-and-comment resilience to conflict and inequality
rubrics_metrics.description: Notice-and-comment rulemaking must contend with pervasive political conflict and unequal capacities to participate; in practice it is 'heavily burdened by conflict and inequality' including mass-commenting campaigns and resource imbalances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate notice-and-comment procedures by whether they (a) handle mass or coordinated commenting in ways that preserve meaningful input, (b) mitigate advantages of well-resourced actors, and (c) maintain deliberative or justificatory quality rather than devolving into performative or captive comment streams.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design for polarized and fractured publics
rubrics_metrics.description: High affective polarization, political extremism, and declining institutional trust make finding a working consensus more difficult; institutional design must account for social fracturing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing reforms to administrative participation, consider whether they are robust to partisan polarization (e.g., avoid procedures that easily become 'blood sport' or hardball tactics) and whether they improve cross-partisan legitimacy rather than exacerbating antagonism.
